name: Gahat ki Dal
subtitle: kumaoni horse gram simmered long and dark, earthy and warming for a cold night

ingredients.note: gahat or kulth — the hill winter pulse
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free
the traditional thickener if the dal stays thin

prepNotes: Soak the horse gram overnight, at least 10 hours. It is the hardest pulse in an Indian kitchen and nothing shortens that.
Discard the soaking water and rinse twice — it carries most of what makes gahat heavy to digest.
In the hills the leftover cooking liquid is drunk on its own as a peppery broth, so keep it thin enough to pour.

steps.text: Pressure cook the drained horse gram with 1.2 litres water, the turmeric and 1 tsp salt for 6 whistles, then simmer on low pressure 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Fewer than 6 whistles and the grains stay stubbornly hard in the middle.

steps.text: Let the pressure fall by itself, then check: a grain should crush easily between finger and thumb. If not, give it 3 more whistles.
Heat the mustard oil in a separate pan until it smokes, cut the heat for a minute, then crackle the cumin and red chillies.
Add the hing, then the crushed garlic and ginger, and fry 90 seconds until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet.
steps.tip: Garlic browner than pale gold turns the dal bitter over the long simmer.

steps.text: Add the onion and cook 7 minutes to a soft light brown, then the tomato and cook 4 minutes until it collapses.
Stir in the coriander powder and chilli powder and fry 1 minute until the oil separates at the edges.
Tip the whole tempering into the cooked dal, stir well and simmer uncovered 20 minutes so the flavours settle in.
steps.tip: This uncovered simmer is where gahat gets its depth. Do not cut it short.

steps.text: If it is still watery, stir in the rice flour slurry and cook 3 minutes until it just coats a spoon.
Check the salt, scatter coriander and serve with rice and a spoon of ghee if you are not keeping it vegan.

storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well for a month. Reheat with plenty of water — it sets almost solid when cold.
